question: The EU’s Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU) generally exempts passenger transport from the general 14-day right of withdrawal (see Article 3(3)(k)). This means that consumers who mistakenly purchase air tickets online do not have a general statutory right to cancel the purchase shortly after payment.

At the same time, digital booking processes can be designed in ways that increase the risk of unintended purchases: travel dates can be pre-filled automatically, for example; insufficient emphasis might be placed on essential booking information; or it might not be possible to spot obvious errors before payment.

In the US, an arrangement is in place under certain conditions whereby airlines have to offer either free cancellation within 24 hours or the option of booking a ticket free of charge, also within 24 hours. There is no such general arrangement in the EU. With the above in mind: 1.

Does the Commission take the view that existing EU consumer protection legislation provides sufficient protection for consumers when it comes to unintended purchases that come about because online flight booking processes are misleadlingly or inappropriately designed?

In the context of the upcoming Digital Fairness Act, will the Commission consider tightening up the requirements for transparency and the active confirmation of important booking information, as well as exploring the need for a short cooling-off period that applies to online purchases of air tickets, where necessary through separate legislation?
